Lecture 28

Transform solutions of physical initial-value problems

Lecture objectives

We prove that the transform method is justified, express every motion of the oscillator through its impulse response, solve a struck oscillator and a switched circuit, read causality from poles, and solve a Volterra equation.

Lecture 26 transformed the oscillator equation under the assumption that the motion and its derivatives are transformable, and Lecture 27 inverted transforms. In this last lecture of Part II we prove that the assumption holds, solve physical initial-value problems with the transform, and compare it with the direct method of Lecture 9 and the state-space method of Lectures 10–14. The lecture reads in three stages: the justification of the method and the impulse response (Sections 28.1 and 28.2), worked problems and the Fourier domain (Sections 28.3–28.5), and a Volterra equation and the choice of a method (Sections 28.6 and 28.7).

28.1 Transformable solutions

In Lecture 26 the derivative rule was applied to the motion of the oscillator and to the solution of a system, and its hypotheses required these functions and their derivatives to be transformable. We now prove that they are, for every force that is piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β][0,\beta][0,β] and transformable. As in Lecture 26, a function on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) is piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β][0,\beta][0,β] if it is piecewise continuous there in the sense of Lecture 23. In particular it is bounded on (0,β](0,\beta](0,β] and has a right limit at 0.00. The causal convolution is (f∗g)(t)=∫0tf(τ)g(t−τ) ⁣dτ(f\conv g)(t)=\int_0^tf(\tau)g(t-\tau)\dd\tau(f∗g)(t)=∫0t​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ for t>0,t>0t>0, as in Lecture 26, and ∥A∥\norm A∥A∥ is the column-sum norm of Lecture 11.

Equation (28.4) is Lecture 26’s transformed oscillator equation solved for Q,QQ, now proved without assuming in advance that the motion is transformable. Formula (28.3) says that the impulse response determines every motion: the data enter through hhh and h˙,\dot hh˙, the force through h∗F,h\conv Fh∗F, and each blow through a delayed copy of h.hh.

Proposition 28.4 (Transform solutions). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 28.3, with FFF transformable at c,cc, let q1q_1q1​ be a transformable function, continuous on (0,∞),(0,\infty)(0,∞), whose transform equals the right side of (28.4) on a half-plane Re⁡s>c′.\Re s>c'Res>c′. Then q1q_1q1​ is the motion. The same holds for the solution x\vv xx of Proposition 28.1, componentwise, with (28.2).

Proof. By Theorem 28.3, the motion qqq is transformable and continuous, and its transform is the right side of (28.4). By Lecture 27’s theorem on the uniqueness of the Laplace transform, q1(t)=q(t)q_1(t)=q(t)q1​(t)=q(t) at every t>0t>0t>0 at which q1−qq_1-qq1​−q is continuous, which is every t>0.t>0t>0. The argument for systems is the same. ■

So every method that produces a continuous transformable function with the right transform gives the solution: residue sums (Lecture 27), the delay and convolution rules, or a table read from right to left. The transform method for a problem with constant coefficients therefore has three steps: transform the equation, with the data at 0−;0^-0−; solve the algebraic equation for the transform; find a continuous transformable function with this transform.

28.2 The causal response kernel

We write the forced term of (28.3) with a kernel that lists the field time ttt first and the source time τ\tauτ second, as in Lectures 8 and 13.

Definition 28.5 (Causal response kernel). The causal response kernel of the oscillator mq¨+bq˙+kq=Fm\ddot q+b\dot q+kq=Fmq¨​+bq˙​+kq=F is G(t,τ)=h(t−τ)=1m Θ(t−τ) K(t,τ)(t,τ∈R),G(t,\tau)=h(t-\tau)=\frac1m\,\Heaviside(t-\tau)\,K(t,\tau)\qquad(t,\tau\in\R),G(t,τ)=h(t−τ)=m1​Θ(t−τ)K(t,τ)(t,τ∈R),(28.5) where hhh is its impulse response and KKK is the kernel of Lecture 8 for the normalized equation, which for constant coefficients depends only on t−τ.t-\taut−τ.

The motion from rest under the force FFF is qF(t)=∫0tG(t,τ) F(τ) ⁣dτ=(h∗F)(t)(t>0).q_F(t)=\int_0^tG(t,\tau)\,F(\tau)\dd\tau=(h\conv F)(t)\qquad(t>0).qF​(t)=∫0t​G(t,τ)F(τ)dτ=(h∗F)(t)(t>0).(28.6) The kernel has the following properties.

  • Causality. G(t,τ)=0G(t,\tau)=0G(t,τ)=0 for t<τ:t<\taut<τ: the motion at the time ttt depends only on the force at earlier times.

  • Time-translation invariance. GGG depends only on t−τ,t-\taut−τ, because the coefficients are constant, so the response is a convolution.

  • Impulse response. For fixed τ,\tauτ, the function t↦G(t,τ)t\mapsto G(t,\tau)t↦G(t,τ) is continuous, and its derivative jumps by 1/m1/m1/m at t=τ.t=\taut=τ. By Lecture 22’s jump formula, as in Lecture 22’s struck oscillator, m ∂t2G+b ∂tG+kG=δ(t−τ)in D′(R).m\,\partial_t^2G+b\,\partial_tG+kG=\dirac(t-\tau)\qquad\text{in }\testspace'(\R).m∂t2​G+b∂t​G+kG=δ(t−τ)in D′(R).(28.7)

The factor 1/m1/m1/m in (28.5) is fixed by the jump: mmm times the jump of ∂tG\partial_tG∂t​G at t=τt=\taut=τ equals 1,11, the weight of the delta. For variable coefficients Lecture 8’s kernel K(t,τ)K(t,\tau)K(t,τ) is not a function of t−τ,t-\taut−τ, the response is not a convolution, and the Laplace transform does not apply. Lecture 42 calls such kernels Green’s functions and compares them with the causal kernel (28.5).

28.3 A driven oscillator struck during its motion

Example 28.6 (A driven oscillator struck during its motion). We find the motion of an underdamped oscillator with initial data, a sinusoidal force and a blow, and identify each part of it. 28.5 The causal response in the Fourier domain

The Fourier transform of Lectures 23–25 also describes the response of a damped oscillator, without initial data, and causality can be read from its poles. Let γ>0.\gamma>0γ>0. Then hhh is continuous on R,\RR, with h(0)=0,h(0)=0h(0)=0, and integrable, and Lecture 26 showed, by the bridge with c=0,c=0c=0, that h^(ω)=H(iω)/2π\widehat h(\omega)=H(\iu\omega)/\sqrt{2\pi}h(ω)=H(iω)/2π​ with the course’s convention h^(ω)=(2π)−1/2∫e−iωth(t) ⁣dt.\widehat h(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{-\iu\omega t}h(t)\dd th(ω)=(2π)−1/2∫e−iωth(t)dt. The frequency response H(iω)=(k−mω2+ibω)−1H(\iu\omega)=(k-m\omega^2+\iu b\omega)^{-1}H(iω)=(k−mω2+ibω)−1 is continuous on R,\RR, because its denominator has the imaginary part bω≠0b\omega\ne0bω=0 for ω≠0\omega\ne0ω=0 and the value kkk at ω=0,\omega=0ω=0, and it is bounded by a constant times ω−2\omega^{-2}ω−2 for large ∣ω∣\abs\omega∣ω∣ by Lecture 19’s lemma on bounds for a rational function. So h^\widehat hh is integrable, and Lecture 23’s theorem on Fourier inversion gives, for every t∈R,t\in\Rt∈R, h(t)=12π∫−∞∞eiωtH(iω) ⁣dω,h(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\ee^{\iu\omega t}H(\iu\omega)\dd\omega ,h(t)=2π1​∫−∞∞​eiωtH(iω)dω,(28.17) the integral converging absolutely.

As a function of a complex ω,\omegaω, the frequency response is a quotient of polynomials. The substitution s=iωs=\iu\omegas=iω relates its denominator to the characteristic polynomial: since ms2+bs+k=m(s−λ+)(s−λ−)ms^2+bs+k=m(s-\lambda_+)(s-\lambda_-)ms2+bs+k=m(s−λ+​)(s−λ−​) and iω−λ=i(ω+iλ),\iu\omega-\lambda=\iu(\omega+\iu\lambda)iω−λ=i(ω+iλ), k−mω2+ibω=m(iω−λ+)(iω−λ−)=−m(ω−ω+)(ω−ω−),ω±=−iλ±.k-m\omega^2+\iu b\omega=m(\iu\omega-\lambda_+)(\iu\omega-\lambda_-)=-m(\omega-\omega_+)(\omega-\omega_-),\qquad \omega_\pm=-\iu\lambda_\pm .k−mω2+ibω=m(iω−λ+​)(iω−λ−​)=−m(ω−ω+​)(ω−ω−​),ω±​=−iλ±​. For γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 both characteristic roots have negative real parts, so Im⁡ω±=−Re⁡λ±>0\Im\omega_\pm=-\Re\lambda_\pm>0Imω±​=−Reλ±​>0 in every damping regime. In the underdamped case ω±=±ωd+iγ.\omega_\pm=\pm\omega_{\mathrm d}+\iu\gammaω±​=±ωd​+iγ. The left half-plane Re⁡s<0\Re s<0Res<0 corresponds to the upper half-plane Im⁡ω>0.\Im\omega>0Imω>0.

We evaluate (28.17) for the underdamped oscillator by Lecture 19’s proposition on rational integrals with an oscillating factor, with ω\omegaω as the real variable and ttt as its parameter. By the factorization above, H(iω)H(\iu\omega)H(iω) is the constant numerator −1/m-1/m−1/m divided by the polynomial (ω−ω+)(ω−ω−),(\omega-\omega_+)(\omega-\omega_-)(ω−ω+​)(ω−ω−​), whose degree exceeds that of the numerator by two and which has no real zeros, because Im⁡ω±=γ>0.\Im\omega_\pm=\gamma>0Imω±​=γ>0.

For t>0t>0t>0 the proposition sums the residues in the upper half-plane, where both poles lie: ∫−∞∞eiωtH(iω) ⁣dω=2πi(−1m)(eiω+tω+−ω−+eiω−tω−−ω+)=−2πim⋅e−γt 2isin⁡ωdt2ωd=2πmωd e−γtsin⁡ωdt,\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^\infty\ee^{\iu\omega t}H(\iu\omega)\dd\omega &=2\pi\iu\Bigl(-\frac1m\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{\ee^{\iu\omega_+t}}{\omega_+-\omega_-}+\frac{\ee^{\iu\omega_-t}}{\omega_--\omega_+}\Bigr)\\ &=-\frac{2\pi\iu}m\cdot\frac{\ee^{-\gamma t}\,2\iu\sin\omega_{\mathrm d}t}{2\omega_{\mathrm d}} =\frac{2\pi}{m\omega_{\mathrm d}}\,\ee^{-\gamma t}\sin\omega_{\mathrm d}t , \end{aligned}∫−∞∞​eiωtH(iω)dω​=2πi(−m1​)(ω+​−ω−​eiω+​t​+ω−​−ω+​eiω−​t​)=−m2πi​⋅2ωd​e−γt2isinωd​t​=mωd​2π​e−γtsinωd​t,​ because ω+−ω−=2ωd\omega_+-\omega_-=2\omega_{\mathrm d}ω+​−ω−​=2ωd​ and eiω±t=e−γte±iωdt.\ee^{\iu\omega_\pm t}=\ee^{-\gamma t}\ee^{\pm\iu\omega_{\mathrm d}t}eiω±​t=e−γte±iωd​t. Division by 2π2\pi2π gives the impulse response h(t)=e−γtsin⁡(ωdt)/(mωd)h(t)=\ee^{-\gamma t}\sin(\omega_{\mathrm d}t)/(m\omega_{\mathrm d})h(t)=e−γtsin(ωd​t)/(mωd​) of Lecture 26. For t<0t<0t<0 the proposition sums the residues in the lower half-plane. There are none, so h(t)=0:h(t)=0h(t)=0: the response vanishes before the impulse because the poles lie in the upper half-plane. ◃

The position of the poles depends on the sign in the exponent of the forward transform. In the positive-forward convention of some older texts, the card of Lecture 23 gives h^+(ω)=h^(−ω)=H(−iω)/2π,\widehat h_+(\omega)=\widehat h(-\omega)=H(-\iu\omega)/\sqrt{2\pi}h+​(ω)=h(−ω)=H(−iω)/2π​, with poles −ω±-\omega_\pm−ω±​ in the lower half-plane. A pole sign from another source must be converted with the card. In the undamped case γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 the poles lie on the real axis, hhh is not integrable, and Lecture 23’s transform does not apply, while the Laplace transform does.

28.6 A Volterra integral equation

Lecture 25’s convolution equations on the whole time axis needed an invertibility condition. Equations in which the unknown at the time ttt depends only on its values at earlier times need no such condition, as we now prove.

Definition 28.9 (Volterra convolution equation). Let the kernel KKK and the function fff be piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β],[0,\beta][0,β], and let λ∈C.\lambda\in\Cλ∈C. A solution of the Volterra convolution equation of the second kind y(t)=f(t)+λ∫0tK(t−τ) y(τ) ⁣dτ(t>0),y(t)=f(t)+\lambda\int_0^tK(t-\tau)\,y(\tau)\dd\tau\qquad(t>0),y(t)=f(t)+λ∫0t​K(t−τ)y(τ)dτ(t>0),(28.18) that is, y=f+λ K∗y,y=f+\lambda\,K\conv yy=f+λK∗y, is a function yyy that is piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β][0,\beta][0,β] and satisfies (28.18).

Here KKK and λ\lambdaλ are as in Lecture 25, not the kernel K(t,τ),K(t,\tau)K(t,τ), the stiffness matrix, λ±\lambda_\pmλ±​ or λj\lambda_jλj​ above. Second kind means that the unknown also appears outside the integral.

The proof below uses two facts about causal convolutions of functions that are piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β].[0,\beta][0,β]. First, such a convolution is continuous on (0,∞):(0,\infty)(0,∞): on (0,β](0,\beta](0,β] it depends only on the factors on (0,β),(0,\beta)(0,β), and the functions equal to them there and to 000 for t≥βt\ge\betat≥β are transformable at every real c,cc, so Lecture 26’s convolution rule applies. The second fact is the following rule.

Lemma 28.10 (Associativity of causal convolution). Let f1,f_1f1​, f2f_2f2​ and f3f_3f3​ be piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β].[0,\beta][0,β]. Then (f1∗f2)∗f3=f1∗(f2∗f3)(f_1\conv f_2)\conv f_3=f_1\conv(f_2\conv f_3)(f1​∗f2​)∗f3​=f1​∗(f2​∗f3​) on (0,∞).(0,\infty)(0,∞).

28.7 Choosing a method

Parts I and II have developed four descriptions of linear response with constant coefficients. The table compares them.

MethodNeedsSuited toCosts
Direct (Lectures 7–9)characteristic roots; a particular solution for each forcingone switching time; forcing by exponentials and sinusoidsa matching of the data at every switching time
State space (Lectures 10–14)the matrix A,AA, its propagator etA\ee^{tA}etA and Duhamel’s formulasystems and networks; all state variables at once; modes and stabilityeigenvectors or a matrix exponential
Laplace transform (Lectures 26–28)a transformable input; the data at 0−0^-0−impulses, delays, switching, convolutions, Volterra equationsfinding a signal with a given transform (residues, Lecture 27)
Fourier transform (Lectures 23–25)an integrable causal impulse response; for the oscillator, positive dampingsteady spectra, filters on the whole time axisno initial data; no undamped or unstable systems

Impulses, delays or several switching times call for the Laplace transform, and coupled variables, modes and stability for the state space. One switching time with exponential or sinusoidal forcing is often quickest by the direct method.

Summary

The solutions of constant-coefficient initial-value problems with inputs that are piecewise continuous on every bounded interval and transformable are transformable. So a continuous transformable function with the transform found from the equation and the data at 0−0^-0− is, by uniqueness, the solution.

1. The dimensionless initial-value problem is y¨+2y˙+y=0\ddot y+2\dot y+y=0y¨​+2y˙​+y=0 for t>0t>0t>0, with y(0+)=1y(0^+)=1y(0+)=1 and y˙(0+)=2\dot y(0^+)=2y˙​(0+)=2. Use the one-sided Laplace transform of this ordinary motion to find y(1)y(1)y(1). Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Transform each derivative with its initial terms, then split the rational expression by powers of its repeated factor.

The initial terms give (s+1)2Y=s+4(s+1)^2Y=s+4(s+1)2Y=s+4. Writing s+4=(s+1)+3s+4=(s+1)+3s+4=(s+1)+3 gives Y=1/(s+1)+3/(s+1)2Y=1/(s+1)+3/(s+1)^2Y=1/(s+1)+3/(s+1)2. The inverse for positive time is y(t)=(1+3t)e−ty(t)=(1+3t)\ee^{-t}y(t)=(1+3t)e−t, with value 111 and derivative 222 at the initial instant. At t=1t=1t=1 it gives 4/e4/\ee4/e. Dropping an initial term changes the coefficient of the repeated-pole contribution.

2. A damped oscillator has H(s)=1/(s2+2s+5)H(s)=1/(s^2+2s+5)H(s)=1/(s2+2s+5) in dimensionless variables. For real frequencies, its frequency response H(iω)H(\iu\omega)H(iω) equals 2π h^(ω)\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat h(\omega)2π​h(ω) in the course’s negative-forward Fourier convention, where hhh is the impulse response. Where are the poles of the frequency response as a function of complex ω\omegaω?

Hint. Find the characteristic roots in sss, then solve s=iωs=\iu\omegas=iω for ω\omegaω.

The denominator is (s+1)2+4(s+1)^2+4(s+1)2+4, so the sss-poles are −1±2i-1\pm2\iu−1±2i. Multiplying by −i-\iu−i gives ω=±2+i\omega=\pm2+\iuω=±2+i. The upper-half-plane positions are consistent with closing above for positive time in the inverse Fourier integral. Multiplying by i\iui would give the lower pair. Leaving the roots unchanged uses the wrong variable, and exchanging the decay rate and oscillation frequency gives the last pair.

3. In a series RLC circuit with constant positive R,L,CR,L,CR,L,C, the applied voltage makes a finite step at t=t0t=t_0t=t0​ with no impulse. If you solve the scalar charge equation separately before and after the switch, which data from the state vector must be carried across continuously?

Hint. Integrate the two first-order state equations over a shrinking interval about the switch.

For the state (Q,I)(Q,I)(Q,I) with I=Q˙I=\dot QI=Q˙​, the equations Q˙=I\dot Q=IQ˙​=I and LI˙=V(t)−RI−Q/CL\dot I=V(t)-RI-Q/CLI˙=V(t)−RI−Q/C have right-hand sides that stay bounded through a finite voltage step. Their integrals across a shrinking interval vanish, so both charge and current have zero jump. The step can change the right limit of Q¨\ddot QQ¨​. It supplies no impulse to change Q˙\dot QQ˙​, and there is no current impulse to change QQQ. Use both left limits as initial data for the scalar equation after the switch.

4. For t≥0t\ge0t≥0 solve y(t)=1+2∫0te−(t−τ)y(τ) ⁣dτy(t)=1+2\int_0^t\ee^{-(t-\tau)}y(\tau)\dd\tauy(t)=1+2∫0t​e−(t−τ)y(τ)dτ by Laplace transformation. Which is the solution?

Hint. Transform the causal convolution and choose a half-plane sufficiently far to the right before dividing.

The equation gives [1−2/(s+1)]Y=1/s[1-2/(s+1)]Y=1/s[1−2/(s+1)]Y=1/s. For Re⁡s>1\Re s>1Res>1 the multiplier is nonzero and Y=(s+1)/[s(s−1)]=2/(s−1)−1/sY=(s+1)/[s(s-1)]=2/(s-1)-1/sY=(s+1)/[s(s−1)]=2/(s−1)−1/s. The inverse is 2et−12\ee^t-12et−1. A zero at s=1s=1s=1 is allowed because the division takes place to its right, and the Volterra theorem gives uniqueness without a separate invertibility hypothesis. The constant ignores feedback. The single exponential misses the forcing contribution. The decaying expression comes from reversing the feedback sign.
